title: Termination of pregnancy and related law
blurb: Know the lawful grounds for termination across the UK and exactly what conscientious objection does and does not cover.
question: Ruth, a labour ward midwife with a conscientious objection to abortion, is allocated a woman having an induction at 22 weeks for a serious fetal anomaly. What must Ruth do, and which tasks may she still be required to perform?

teach.body: Formally, the Abortion Act 1967 s1 provides that no offence is committed when a registered medical practitioner terminates a pregnancy and two registered medical practitioners have formed, in good faith, the opinion that a listed ground applies. In plain English: termination is lawful in Great Britain when two doctors agree one of four grounds is met, and it is carried out in an NHS hospital or approved place.

head: Ground
In short
Time limit
rows: Risk to her or existing children's health greater than termination
Necessary to prevent grave permanent injury
Risk to her life greater than termination
Substantial risk of serious fetal abnormality
teach.caption: s1(4): in an emergency to save life or prevent grave permanent injury, one practitioner's opinion is enough.
In NI a 'registered medical professional' includes a registered midwife or nurse (reg 2).

teach.body: Section 4(1): no one is under a duty to participate in treatment authorised by the Act to which they have a conscientious objection. The burden of proving it rests on the objector. Section 4(2): the right does not apply where treatment is necessary to save the life or prevent grave permanent injury to the woman. Code 4.4: tell colleagues, your manager and the woman, and arrange a suitably qualified colleague to take over.

teach.h: Scenario: Ruth on the labour ward
teach.body: Ruth tells the coordinator and her manager of her objection and, as Code 4.4 requires, ensures the woman's care passes to a suitably qualified colleague without delay. She does not share her personal views with the woman (Code 20.7). If the woman later haemorrhaged and Ruth was needed to save her life, s4(2) means she must act. Once the birth is over, ordinary observations and comfort care are outside s4, so Ruth may be asked to give them.

early medical abortion pills at home (E&W)
NI: no ground needed up to this point

teach.caption: s1(3D): pills may be taken at home in England or Wales after a consultation with a doctor, nurse or midwife.

teach.text: The 24-week limit belongs to ground (a). Grounds (b), (c) and (d), including serious fetal anomaly, have no time limit. And the Abortion Act does not extend to Northern Ireland: NI uses the 2020 Regulations.

teach.body: Midwives promote women's sexual and reproductive rights (SPM 1.3). A woman considering termination at first contact should be offered referral to sexual health services (CG110 1.1.11). Since 29 April 2026, in England and Wales, no offence is committed by a woman acting in relation to her own pregnancy (Crime and Policing Act 2026 s241). The Abortion Act rules for providers are unchanged.
teach.cite: SPM 1.3; NICE CG110 1.1.11; Crime and Policing Act 2026 s241

items: GB: two practitioners, four grounds; 24 weeks for ground (a), no limit for (b) to (d).
NI: 2020 Regulations; up to 12 weeks with no ground, midwives count as registered medical professionals.
s4 objection: hands-on participation, burden on the objector, not in an emergency to save life.
Code 4.4: tell colleagues, manager and the woman; hand over to a suitably qualified colleague.
Booking, allocating staff and ordinary aftercare are not covered (Doogan).

summary: You can now state the lawful grounds for termination in Great Britain and Northern Ireland and their time limits. You can also apply conscientious objection correctly: what it covers, what it does not, and how to hand over care safely.

A.q: Under the Abortion Act 1967, how many registered medical practitioners must form the opinion that ground (a) applies in a non-emergency termination?
options: Two
One
Three
One doctor and one midwife
A.why: Section 1(1) requires two registered medical practitioners to form the opinion in good faith. One is enough only in the s1(4) emergency.

whyNot.1: One opinion suffices under s1(4) for immediate necessity, not for ground (a).
whyNot.2: The Act requires two opinions, not three.
whyNot.3: In Great Britain the opinions must come from registered medical practitioners, not midwives.

A.q: A woman is offered termination at 25 weeks after scans show a substantial risk of serious fetal abnormality. Which statement about the time limit is correct?
options: The limit for this ground is 24 weeks
The limit for this ground is 28 weeks
There is no time limit for this ground
The limit for this ground is 20 weeks
A.why: Ground (d), substantial risk of serious fetal abnormality, has no gestational limit. The 24-week limit applies to ground (a).

whyNot.0: 24 weeks is the limit for ground (a), not ground (d).
whyNot.1: 28 weeks is not a limit in the current Act.
whyNot.3: 20 weeks is not a statutory limit for any ground.

A.q: Where in the UK does the Abortion Act 1967 apply?
options: England, Wales and Northern Ireland
All four nations of the UK
England and Wales
England, Wales and Scotland
A.why: The Act extends to England, Wales and Scotland. Northern Ireland has its own framework, the Abortion (Northern Ireland) (No. 2) Regulations 2020.

whyNot.0: It does not extend to Northern Ireland, and Scotland is covered.
whyNot.1: It does not extend to Northern Ireland.
whyNot.2: Scotland is also covered by the Act.

B.q: A midwife with a conscientious objection to abortion is allocated a woman admitted for induction for termination. What should she do first?
options: Provide the care, as the right does not extend to midwives
Tell her manager and arrange a qualified colleague to take over
Swap the allocation quietly without giving any reason
Explain her moral objection to the woman in some detail
B.why: Code 4.4: tell colleagues, your manager and the person receiving care, and arrange for a suitably qualified colleague to take over responsibility.

whyNot.0: Section 4 applies to any person, including midwives, who would participate in the treatment.
whyNot.2: The Code requires the objection to be made known so care is handed over safely.
whyNot.3: Code 20.7: do not express personal beliefs to people in an inappropriate way.

B.q: A labour ward coordinator objects to booking in women for termination and allocating midwives to their care. According to the Supreme Court in Doogan, what is the legal position?
options: These tasks are covered, as any involvement counts
These tasks are covered in Scotland but not in England
These tasks are covered once she objects in writing
These tasks are not hands-on, so s4 does not cover them
B.why: Doogan [2014] UKSC 68 held that 'participate' means taking part in a hands-on capacity. Ancillary, administrative and managerial tasks such as booking and allocating are not covered.

whyNot.0: The Supreme Court rejected the wide 'any involvement' interpretation.
whyNot.1: The meaning of s4 is the same throughout Great Britain.
whyNot.2: A written objection does not widen the scope of the statutory right.

B.q: A woman having a medical termination at 18 weeks starts to haemorrhage heavily. The only midwife immediately available has a conscientious objection. What must she do?
options: Give the care needed to save the woman's life
Wait with the woman until a colleague arrives
Call the doctor and leave the room promptly
Give care if the woman requests it in writing
B.why: Section 4(2): the right of objection does not affect any duty to participate in treatment necessary to save the life or prevent grave permanent injury to the woman.

whyNot.1: Waiting delays life-saving care; s4(2) removes the objection in an emergency.
whyNot.2: Leaving a haemorrhaging woman breaches the duty of care and s4(2).
whyNot.3: No written request is needed; the duty arises from the emergency itself.

C.q: Siobhan, who lives in Belfast, is 11 weeks pregnant and asks her midwife about ending the pregnancy. She has no medical complications. Which statement about the law is correct?
options: Termination is unlawful, as the 1967 Act does not apply
Termination is lawful once two doctors certify a s1 ground
Termination is lawful up to 24 weeks without any ground
Termination is lawful up to 12 weeks without a stated ground
C.why: Regulation 3 of the Abortion (Northern Ireland) (No. 2) Regulations 2020 permits termination where a registered medical professional is of the opinion that the pregnancy has not exceeded its 12th week.

whyNot.0: The 1967 Act does not apply, but the 2020 Regulations make termination lawful in NI.
whyNot.1: Section 1 of the 1967 Act does not extend to Northern Ireland.
whyNot.2: Between 12 and 24 weeks the NI Regulations require a health risk ground and two opinions.

C.q: After a termination for fetal anomaly at 20 weeks, the woman is moved to a side room. The midwife with a conscientious objection is asked to do her routine observations and offer comfort. What is the correct position?
options: She may decline, as all aftercare forms part of the treatment
She should provide it, as ordinary nursing care is not covered
She may decline once she explains her beliefs to the woman
She should provide it once her manager confirms it in writing
C.why: Doogan: the ordinary nursing and pastoral care of a woman who has just given birth is outside the scope of s4. Only aftercare specifically required by the process is covered.

whyNot.0: Only specific aftercare arising from the process is covered, not all aftercare.
whyNot.2: Explaining beliefs does not widen s4 and may breach Code 20.7.
whyNot.3: Written confirmation is irrelevant; the legal scope decides the duty.

C.q: Under s1(3B)-(3D) of the Abortion Act, a woman living in England may take early medical abortion pills at home after a consultation with a doctor, nurse or midwife. Up to what gestation?
options: 10 weeks
9 weeks
12 weeks
14 weeks
C.why: The practitioner must be of the opinion that the pregnancy will not exceed ten weeks when the medicine is administered (s1(3B)(b)), with home use permitted by s1(3D).

whyNot.1: Nine weeks is below the statutory figure of ten weeks.
whyNot.2: Twelve weeks is the Northern Ireland no-ground limit, not the home-use limit.
whyNot.3: Fourteen weeks exceeds the ten-week limit in s1(3B).

reteach.title: Two maps and one boundary
reteach.question: Think of the law as two maps (GB and NI) and one boundary line around what an objector can refuse. Where does each fall?

blocks.body: Map one, Great Britain: two doctors, four grounds, 24 weeks for the health ground (a), no limit for the others. Map two, Northern Ireland: 2020 Regulations, 12 weeks with no ground, 24 weeks for health risk, no limit for severe or fatal fetal anomaly. The boundary line: an objector may refuse hands-on treatment, but not booking or allocating, not ordinary aftercare, and not life-saving care.

blocks.text: An objector must still hand over: the Supreme Court said a conscientious objector is obliged to refer to a professional who does not share the objection.

explain.body: Two practitioners agree in good faith that: (a) under 24 weeks, continuing risks injury to her or her existing children's health more than termination; (b) termination prevents grave permanent injury; (c) continuing risks her life more than termination; or (d) substantial risk of serious fetal abnormality.

test.q: At 26 weeks, a woman's pregnancy is found to carry a substantial risk to her life greater than if it were ended. Under which ground could termination lawfully proceed?
options: Ground (a), as it has no limit
Ground (c), which has no time limit
None, as 24 weeks has passed
Ground (d), as it covers her life
test.why: Ground (c), risk to the woman's life greater than if the pregnancy were terminated, has no time limit.

whyNot.3: Ground (d) concerns serious fetal abnormality, not the woman's life.

explain.body: The 1967 Act covers England, Wales and Scotland. Northern Ireland uses the Abortion (Northern Ireland) (No. 2) Regulations 2020, in which registered midwives and nurses count as registered medical professionals. SPM 1.2 expects midwives to distinguish between UK legislatures.

test.q: A midwife moves from Glasgow to a unit in Northern Ireland. Which provision now governs her right of conscientious objection to termination?
options: Section 4 of the Abortion Act 1967
Section 38 of the HFE Act 1990
Standard 4.4 of the NMC Code
Part 7 of the 2020 NI Regulations
test.why: In Northern Ireland the statutory right is in Part 7 (regulation 12) of the Abortion (Northern Ireland) (No. 2) Regulations 2020. Section 4 covers Great Britain only.

whyNot.0: Section 4 of the 1967 Act applies in England, Wales and Scotland.
whyNot.1: HFE Act s38 covers fertility procedures, not termination.
whyNot.2: Code 4.4 sets professional expectations but is not the statutory right.

explain.body: Section 4: no duty to participate if you object, burden of proof on you, but not where treatment is needed to save life or prevent grave permanent injury. Code 4.4: tell colleagues, manager and the woman, and arrange a suitably qualified colleague to take over. Code 20.7: do not express personal beliefs inappropriately.

test.q: Who bears the burden of proving a conscientious objection in legal proceedings under s4?
options: The employing NHS trust
The woman having the termination
The person claiming the objection
The practitioners certifying the ground
test.why: Section 4(1): the burden of proof of conscientious objection rests on the person claiming to rely on it.

whyNot.0: The trust does not have to disprove the objection.
whyNot.1: The woman has no burden in relation to staff objections.
whyNot.3: Certifying practitioners form the s1 opinion; they do not prove others' objections.

explain.body: The Supreme Court held that 'participate' means taking part in a hands-on capacity. It covers the whole course of treatment from induction to delivery, including monitoring labour and pain relief, plus specific aftercare. It does not cover managerial tasks or the ordinary nursing and pastoral care of a woman after birth.

test.q: Which task linked to a termination may an objecting midwife lawfully decline, following Doogan?
options: Allocating a colleague to the woman
Giving her analgesia during the labour
Booking her in on the ward system
Giving routine postnatal comfort care
test.why: Giving pain relief during the labour is hands-on participation in the course of treatment, so s4 covers it (outside an emergency).

whyNot.0: Allocating staff is a managerial task outside s4.
whyNot.2: Booking in is an administrative task outside s4.
whyNot.3: Ordinary pastoral and nursing care after birth is outside s4.
